{
"title": "Reduced residence time of droplet impact on heated surfaces",
"authors": "Song Rong, Shiquan Shen, Tianyou Wang, and Zhizhao Che",
"field_subfield": "Fluid dynamics / multiphase heat transfer",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental and theoretical study",
"executive_summary": "This paper investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, with a focus on reducing the residence time—the interval between the moments a droplet visually contacts and visually detaches from the substrate. The authors identify a new bouncing mode, termed the bouncing-with-spray (BWS) mode, which dramatically shortens the residence time compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing (RB) mode. The BWS mode arises from the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, which creates holes that cause the liquid film to recoil into fragments, thereby reducing the recoiling distance and time. This mechanism is induced by heat, making it simple and reliable, as it avoids surface degradation and complex fabrication of microstructures. The study uses water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, with Weber numbers varied from 10 to 180. The residence time reduction is found to be independent of liquid viscosity, and the BWS mode reduces the residence time by about 40% compared with the RB mode. A theoretical model is proposed to describe the transition between the two modes in the film boiling regime, yielding a scaling law (ΔT ∼ V⁻¹) that agrees well with the experimental data. The model also explains the transition in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into the impact dynamics and potential applications in spray cooling, anti-icing, self-cleaning, and corrosion resistance.",

summary.title: Reduced residence time of droplet impact on heated surfaces
summary.authors: Song Rong, Shiquan Shen, Tianyou Wang, and Zhizhao Che
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, with a focus on reducing the residence time—the interval between the moments a droplet visually contacts and visually detaches from the substrate. The authors identify a new bouncing mode, termed the bouncing-with-spray (BWS) mode, which dramatically shortens the residence time compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing (RB) mode. The BWS mode arises from the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, which creates holes that cause the liquid film to recoil into fragments, thereby reducing the recoiling distance and time. This mechanism is induced by heat, making it simple and reliable, as it avoids surface degradation and complex fabrication of microstructures. The study uses water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, with Weber numbers varied from 10 to 180. The residence time reduction is found to be independent of liquid viscosity, and the BWS mode reduces the residence time by about 40% compared with the RB mode. A theoretical model is proposed to describe the transition between the two modes in the film boiling regime, yielding a scaling law (ΔT ∼ V⁻¹) that agrees well with the experimental data. The model also explains the transition in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into the impact dynamics and potential applications in spray cooling, anti-icing, self-cleaning, and corrosion resistance.

Executive Summary
This paper investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, with a focus on reducing the residence time—the interval between the moments a droplet visually contacts and visually detaches from the substrate. The authors identify a new bouncing mode, termed the bouncing-with-spray (BWS) mode, which dramatically shortens the residence time compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing (RB) mode. The BWS mode arises from the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, which creates holes that cause the liquid film to recoil into fragments, thereby reducing the recoiling distance and time. This mechanism is induced by heat, making it simple and reliable, as it avoids surface degradation and complex fabrication of microstructures. The study uses water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, with Weber numbers varied from 10 to 180. The residence time reduction is found to be independent of liquid viscosity, and the BWS mode reduces the residence time by about 40% compared with the RB mode. A theoretical model is proposed to describe the transition between the two modes in the film boiling regime, yielding a scaling law (ΔT ∼ V⁻¹) that agrees well with the experimental data. The model also explains the transition in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into the impact dynamics and potential applications in spray cooling, anti-icing, self-cleaning, and corrosion resistance.

Research Context
Droplet impact occurs ubiquitously in nature and industrial applications. Impact on heated surfaces is affected by heat transfer and phase change. Reducing contact/residence time is important for various applications. Prior strategies to reduce contact time involve surface modifications. The Leidenfrost effect forms a vapor layer that insulates the droplet. Residence time is a key parameter in the impact process. Film boiling allows droplet bouncing after recoil. Reducing residence time is challenging due to theoretical limits.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to identify a mode that reduces residence time. The BWS mode is hypothesized to reduce residence time significantly. The heat-induced approach is hypothesized to be simple and reliable. The reduction is attributed to vapor bubble burst and film recoil. A scaling law is hypothesized for the transition boundary. The scaling law is expected to agree with experimental data. The model is expected to explain the transition in transition boiling.

Methodological Details
Three liquids were used: water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures. Droplets were injected at approximately 4 µl/s by a syringe pump. Droplets formed at the tip of a blunt syringe needle. Droplets detached when gravity exceeded surface tension. Droplets impacted on a polished silicon substrate heated by a copper holder. Two K-type thermocouples controlled temperature with ±1°C accuracy. Images were captured using a Photron Fastcam SA1.1 high-speed camera. Droplet size was typically 2.8 mm for water-glycerol mixtures. Impact speed ranged from 0.9 to 2.1 m/s. The Weber number ranged from 10 to 180. The Jakob number indicated the ratio of sensible to latent heat. Liquid properties are summarized in Table 1. Viscosity was varied by changing glycerol concentration. Droplet size, impact speed, and shape evolution were measured. The Weber number quantifies the ratio of kinetic to surface energy. The Jakob number is defined as Ja ≡ cp(Tw − Ts)/ℓ. The specific latent heat of vaporization is denoted by ℓ.

Procedures And Architectures
The experimental setup is schematically described in Figure 1. The setup includes a syringe pump, high-speed camera, and LED light source. Side-view and aerial-view images were captured. The impact process was illuminated by an LED light source. The Weber number is defined as We ≡ ρD0V²/σ. The residence time is defined as the interval between visual contact and detachment. In nucleate boiling, vapor bubbles form immediately upon impact. In transition boiling, an unstable vapor film may exist. In film boiling, a stable vapor film forms immediately upon impact. The critical condition for transition is when bubble radius equals film thickness. The minimum film thickness is given by bmin ∼ Re⁻²/⁵ D0. The heat transfer area to the vapor bubble is regarded as a constant. The scaling exponent n is 0.35 for this study. The scaling law is ΔT ∼ V⁻¹. The scaling law agrees well with the experimental data. The model explains the transition in the transition boiling regime.

Key Results
The BWS mode reduces residence time compared with the RB mode. In transition boiling, the residence time is 6.5 ms vs. 12.0 ms. In film boiling, the residence time is 6.3 ms vs. 12.0 ms. The BWS mode reduces residence time by about 40%. The residence time in the RB mode is about 2.3. The residence time in the BWS mode is about 1.4. The residence time reduction is independent of viscosity. The BWS mode was observed for all kinds of liquids. The scaling exponent n is 0.35. The exponent is close to that in the study of Tran et al. The transition temperature increases with We in the transition boiling regime. The critical We increases with the substrate temperature. The scaling law agrees well with the experimental data. The model explains the transition in the transition boiling regime.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The BWS mode is caused by the burst of vapor bubbles. The burst creates holes in the liquid film. The holes cause the liquid film to recoil into fragments. The reduced recoiling distance shortens the residence time. The mechanism is similar to that on superhydrophobic surfaces with ridges. The scaling law provides a theoretical framework. The model explains the transition in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into the impact dynamics. The findings can help optimize the process in relevant applications. The BWS mode is reliable and easy to achieve.
